title: The Dao, Wu Wei and Yin-Yang
bigQuestion: What does it mean to go with the Way instead of forcing things?

story.title: Stop Fighting the Water
story.kicker: A swimmer stops fighting a strong current and floats safely to shore.
paragraphs: Jada was swimming in Lake Michigan on a windy summer day. She had gone out farther than she meant to. When she turned back, the water pulled her sideways along the beach. She kicked hard toward shore. She got nowhere.

Her arms grew tired. Her heart pounded. Then she remembered what the lifeguard had told her class: 'If a current pulls you, don't fight it head-on. Float. Swim across it, along the shore. Then come in.'
Jada rolled onto her back and floated. She breathed slowly. Then she swam sideways, with easy strokes, parallel to the beach. Little by little, the pull let go. She turned and swam in.
On the sand, she sat wrapped in a towel. The lifeguard sat beside her. 'You did it right,' he said. 'Fighting the water wears you out. Working with it gets you home.'
Jada thought about that for a long time. Her grandmother had once shown her an old Chinese book that talked about water, and about acting without forcing. Now she wanted to read it again.
story.think: When have you gotten further by working with something instead of fighting it?

lessons.title: A Way Without a Name
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the Dao is beyond names; 'Dao,' the Way, is only a word used to point to it.
reading: *Dao* means way, road or path. Confucius used it for the right way to live and govern. The Daodejing uses it for something larger: the source and pattern of everything.
In chapter 25, the Daodejing describes something that existed before heaven and earth. It says: I do not know its name. I call it Dao. If I must describe it, I call it great.
So the book says Dao is not really a name. It is a word to point at something words cannot hold. Readers compare it to a finger pointing at the moon: look at the moon, not the finger.

words.d: the Way; in the Daodejing, the nameless source and pattern of all things

look.title: Daodejing 25
look.text: There was something formed before heaven and earth. It was still and without form. I do not know its name. I call it the Dao. If forced to describe it, I call it great.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 25, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Tao Teh King, 1891)
look.prompt: Why does the speaker say he does not know its name?

check.q: What does Dao mean?
check.why: Dao means way or path.

check.q: What does Daodejing 25 say about the Dao's name?
choices: I do not know its name; I call it Dao
check.why: Chapter 25 says the speaker does not know its name.

check.q: How did Confucius use the word Dao?
choices: For the source of all things only
For the right way to live and govern
check.why: Confucius used Dao for the right way of living and governing.

lessons.title: One, Two, Three, All Things
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing 42 says the Dao gives rise to one, two, three and all things.
reading: Chapter 42 of the Daodejing has a short, famous line. The Dao gave birth to one. One gave birth to two. Two gave birth to three. Three gave birth to all things.
The chapter does not explain exactly what one, two and three are. Readers have offered many answers. Many say two means yin and yang, which the same chapter goes on to name.
The big idea is that everything comes from the Dao. The Daodejing calls the Dao the mother of all things in chapter 1 and elsewhere. Things arise, grow and return to it.

words.d: one reader's explanation of what a text means

look.title: Daodejing 42
look.text: The Dao produced One. One produced Two. Two produced Three. Three produced all things.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 42, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: What might 'two' stand for? Why do readers disagree about it?

check.q: In Daodejing 42, what does three produce?
check.why: The chapter says three produced all things.

check.q: What do many readers say 'two' means in chapter 42?
check.why: The same chapter goes on to name yin and yang.

check.q: What is an interpretation?
choices: One reader's explanation of what a text means
check.why: Different readers give different interpretations.

lessons.title: Following What Is Natural
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the Dao follows ziran, what is 'so of itself,' or natural.
reading: Chapter 25 ends with a chain. People follow the earth. The earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Dao. And the Dao follows *ziran*. It is one of the book's best-known lines.
Ziran literally means 'so of itself.' It is often translated as natural or spontaneous. It describes things happening by their own nature, without being pushed.
Daoist readers often point to nature as a teacher. Seasons change on their own. Rivers find their way downhill. The Daodejing asks readers to notice this kind of ease.

words.d: 'so of itself'; being natural or spontaneous, happening by its own nature
happening naturally, without being planned or forced

look.title: Nature Without Pushing
look.text: No one pushes the maple trees on your street to turn red in October. No one pulls the rain down to the ground. Birds fly south without a map. The Daodejing calls this kind of happening ziran.
look.prompt: Name one more thing in nature that happens 'so of itself.'

check.q: What does ziran literally mean?
check.why: Ziran means 'so of itself,' natural.

check.q: In chapter 25, what does the Dao follow?
check.why: The chain ends: the Dao follows ziran.

check.q: What does spontaneous mean?
check.why: Spontaneous means happening on its own.

lessons.title: Doing Without Forcing
lessons.mainIdea: Wu wei means acting without forcing; the Daodejing says the Dao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.
reading: *Wu wei* literally means 'not doing' or 'no action.' But it does not mean being lazy. Scholars explain it as acting without forcing, strain or grabbing.
Chapter 37 says the Dao does nothing, and yet nothing is left undone. Things grow and change without the Dao pushing them. The Daodejing suggests people can act that way too.
Think of an expert. A skilled dancer or basketball player moves smoothly. They do not look like they are forcing it. Many readers use this as a picture of wu wei.

words.d: acting without forcing; effortless action that goes with the way things are

look.title: Daodejing 37
look.text: The Dao does nothing, and yet there is nothing it does not do.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 37, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: How can something 'do nothing' and still get everything done?

check.q: What does wu wei mean, as scholars explain it?
check.why: Wu wei means acting without forcing, not laziness.

check.q: What does chapter 37 say about the Dao?
choices: It does nothing, yet nothing is left undone
check.why: Chapter 37 gives this paradox.

check.q: Which is a good picture of wu wei?
check.why: Skilled, unforced action is a common picture of wu wei.

lessons.title: The Swimmer at the Waterfall
lessons.mainIdea: In a Zhuangzi story, a swimmer survives a huge waterfall by going with the water, not against it.
reading: The Zhuangzi, chapter 19, tells of Confucius at a great waterfall. The water fell so far and so fast that no fish or turtle could swim there. Then he saw a man in the water.
Confucius thought the man was in trouble. He sent students to help. But the man came out, singing, and walked along the bank. Confucius asked how he did it.

The man said he went down with the swirls and came up with the currents. He followed the water's way and did not force his own. Readers see wu wei in this story. Note that the Zhuangzi often places Confucius in its own stories.

words.d: a Daoist thinker of about the 300s BCE, and the book of stories named after him

look.title: The Swimmer
look.text: Confucius asked the swimmer his secret. The man said: I go down with the whirl and come up with the swirl. I follow the way of the water and do not put myself in charge.
look.cite: Zhuangzi, chapter 19, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Writings of Kwang-ze, 1891)
look.prompt: How is this swimmer like Jada in the opening story?

check.q: Which book tells the story of the swimmer at the waterfall?
check.why: It is in Zhuangzi chapter 19.

check.q: How did the swimmer survive?
choices: He went with the water's way
check.why: He followed the water and did not force his own way.

check.q: Who watches the swimmer in the story?
check.why: The Zhuangzi places Confucius at the waterfall.

lessons.title: Leading Without Forcing
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing says the best leaders are barely noticed, so people feel they did the work themselves.
reading: Chapter 17 of the Daodejing ranks leaders. The best leader, it says, is one the people barely know is there. The next best is loved and praised. Worse is one who is feared.
When the best leader's work is done, the chapter says, the people all say: we did this ourselves. The leader has helped without taking over. The leader's help is real, but it stays in the background.
Readers apply this to many kinds of leading. Coaches, teachers and team captains talk about it. They set things up so others can do their best, without forcing them.

words.d: a person who guides a group
not boastful; not trying to be the center of attention

look.title: Chapter 17's Ranking of Leaders
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 17, following James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Why might a leader people barely notice be ranked best?

check.q: Which leader does chapter 17 rank best?
choices: One the people barely know is there
check.why: Chapter 17 ranks the barely-noticed leader first.

check.q: What do the people say when the best leader's work is done?
check.why: They say they did it themselves.

check.q: What does humble mean?
check.why: Humble means not trying to be the center of attention.

sections.title: Yin, Yang, De and Daoist Practice

lessons.title: Yin and Yang
lessons.mainIdea: Yin and yang are paired opposites that need each other; later artists drew them in the taijitu symbol.
reading: *Yin* first meant the shady side of a hill. *Yang* meant the sunny side. Chinese thinkers came to use them for all pairs of opposites: dark and light, cool and warm, rest and motion.
Yin and yang are not good and evil. They need each other and keep changing into each other. Night turns into day, and day into night. Chapter 42 of the Daodejing names them together.
The swirling black-and-white circle is called the *taijitu*. Early forms of this diagram appear in the Song dynasty, about 1,000 years ago. The familiar swirl took shape later still.

words.d: paired opposites, like shade and sun, that need each other and change into each other
the diagram of yin and yang, often drawn as a swirling circle

look.title: Opposites That Need Each Other
look.text: Picture a hill at sunrise. The east side glows in sunlight: yang. The west side lies in shadow: yin. By evening, the sun has moved. Now the west side is bright and the east is shady. The hill is the same. The sides trade places.
look.prompt: How does this picture show that yin and yang change into each other?

check.q: What did yin first mean?
choices: The shady side of a hill
The sunny side of a hill
check.why: Yin first meant the shady side; yang the sunny side.

check.q: Are yin and yang the same as good and evil?
choices: No, they are paired opposites that need each other
check.why: They are complementary, not good versus evil.

check.q: What is the taijitu?
choices: The diagram of yin and yang
check.why: The taijitu is the yin-yang diagram.

lessons.title: De: Power and Virtue
lessons.mainIdea: De means the power or virtue a thing has when it follows the Dao; the Daodejing says Dao gives life and de nourishes it.
reading: *De* is the second word in the book's title. It is often translated as power, virtue or potency. Legge translated it as virtue. It names the power that the Way gives to things.
In the Daodejing, de is the quiet strength that comes from following the Dao. It is not power over others. It is more like the power a seed has to grow.

Chapter 51 says the Dao gives things life and de nourishes them. Confucius also used the word de, for the good character of a ruler or a junzi. The two traditions share the word but stress different things.

words.d: power or virtue; in the Daodejing, the quiet strength of following the Dao

look.title: Daodejing 51
look.text: The Dao gives all things life. De nourishes them. They take shape and grow. So all things honor the Dao and value de.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 51, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: In this chapter, what is the job of the Dao and what is the job of de?

check.q: How did Legge translate de?
check.why: Legge translated de as virtue.

check.q: In Daodejing 51, what does de do?
check.why: The Dao gives life and de nourishes.

check.q: How is de like a seed's power?
choices: It is quiet strength to grow
check.why: Readers compare de to the inner strength to grow, not power over others.

lessons.title: Philosophy and Religion
lessons.mainIdea: Daoism is studied as a philosophy, and for many people it is also a living religion with temples, priests and rituals.
reading: Some people read the Daodejing and Zhuangzi as philosophy, a way of thinking about life. Others practice Daoism as a religion. Daoist communities have temples, priests, scriptures and festivals.

Tradition says an organized Daoist movement, the Way of the Celestial Masters, began around 142 CE. Daoist believers honor Laozi as a deity. Priests lead rituals, and many Daoists practice meditation and exercises for health.
Scholars used to split Daoism into 'philosophical' and 'religious.' Many now say the line is not so sharp. Daoist priests have read the Daodejing as scripture for many centuries.

words.d: the study of big questions about life, knowledge and right and wrong
a set of beliefs and practices shared by a community, often about the sacred
an early organized Daoist movement, traditionally dated to about 142 CE

look.title: A Visit to a Daoist Temple
look.text: A family walks into a Daoist temple during New Year. Incense smoke drifts past red columns. A statue of Laozi sits calmly in one hall. A priest in a robe chants from a scripture. People bow and leave offerings of fruit.
look.prompt: Which parts of this scene are practices of Daoist religion? How are the visitors showing respect?

check.q: Which is true of Daoism?
choices: It is only a museum subject
It is studied as philosophy and practiced as a religion
check.why: Daoism is both a philosophy people study and a living religion.

check.q: About when does tradition date the Celestial Masters?
check.why: Tradition dates the movement to about 142 CE.

check.q: How do Daoist believers honor Laozi?
check.why: Daoist believers honor Laozi as a deity.

review.q: What does Daodejing 25 say about the Dao's name?
choices: The speaker does not know it and calls it Dao
review.why: Chapter 25 says the name is unknown; Dao is a word used for it.
Wu wei means unforced action, not laziness.

review.why: The best leader is barely known to the people.

choices: Paired opposites that need each other

review.q: What does de mean in the Daodejing?

review.why: De is the quiet strength of following the Dao.

review.q: What do many scholars now say about 'philosophical' and 'religious' Daoism?

review.why: Daoist priests have long read the Daodejing as scripture.
